\chapter{Farewells}
\label{ch:it-farewells}
\hlchaptermodality{4}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can close an Italian conversation and pick the goodbye that matches when I will next see the person.}

Open with ciao, ask Come stai?, then choose the exit — a più tardi within the hour, a domani for tomorrow, a presto for soon, arrivederci for until-we-meet-again.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[arrivederci]{arrivederci — \textquotedblleft{}goodbye,\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}until we meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:IT-C04-arrivederci}



\begin{quote}
You can open a conversation in Italian and ask how someone is. Now, close it. The standard goodbye is \textbf{arrivederci} — and, like its French and German cousins, it doesn't say \textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{} at all. It says \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}until we see each other again.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{arrivederci} = \emph{ar-ree-veh-\textbf{DER}-chee}: a tapped double \emph{r}, and the final \emph{-ci} is soft (\emph{chee}, Italian \emph{c} before \emph{i}). Stress the \emph{-der-}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
Break it into four pieces you can almost read straight off:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a} = \textquotedblleft{}to / until\textquotedblright{} (Latin \emph{ad}).
  \item \textbf{ri-} = \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} (Latin \emph{re-} — as in English \emph{re}-do, \emph{re}-view).
  \item \textbf{vedere} = \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} (Latin \emph{vidēre} $\to$ English \textbf{video}, \textbf{vision}, \textbf{evident}, \textbf{provide}).
  \item \textbf{-ci} = \textquotedblleft{}us / each other.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Glued: \emph{a-(ri)-vedere-ci} $\to$ \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}to our seeing-one-another-again.\textquotedblright{}} You don't say farewell; you promise the next meeting.

\#\#\# The whole family says the same thing

This \textquotedblleft{}until re-seeing\textquotedblright{} idea is shared right across the languages you're learning — a lovely thing to notice:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{goodbye} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Italian} & \emph{arrivederci} & \textquotedblleft{}to our re-seeing\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{French} & \emph{au revoir} & \textquotedblleft{}to the re-seeing\textquotedblright{} (\emph{re} + \emph{voir}, see) \\
\textbf{German} & \emph{auf Wiedersehen} & \textquotedblleft{}on again-seeing\textquotedblright{} (\emph{wieder} + \emph{sehen}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three languages, one gesture: part by pointing at the reunion, not the parting. (Italian keeps a heavier, final \textquotedblleft{}to God\textquotedblright{} goodbye too — \textbf{addio}, \emph{a Dio} — the exact twin of Spanish \emph{adiós}; but for everyday partings it's \emph{arrivederci}.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}arrivederci\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ar-ree-veh-DER-chee}
  \item arrivederci / au revoir / auf Wiedersehen — all \textquotedblleft{}until we see again\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vedere\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}video, vision\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{see} root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{arrivederci} literally promise? (\textquotedblleft{}Until we see each other again.\textquotedblright{}) What French and German goodbyes share that exact idea? (\emph{au revoir}, \emph{auf Wiedersehen}.) Which heavier Italian goodbye means \textquotedblleft{}to God,\textquotedblright{} like Spanish \emph{adiós}? (\emph{addio}.) Next: \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{a domani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a domani]{a domani — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:IT-C04-a-domani}



\begin{quote}
The \textquotedblleft{}until re-seeing\textquotedblright{} pattern gives you a whole family of goodbyes: just name \textbf{when}. First: \textbf{a domani}, \textquotedblleft{}to tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a domani} = \emph{ah doh-\textbf{MAH}-nee}: clean open vowels, stress the \emph{-ma-}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a} = \textquotedblleft{}to / until\textquotedblright{} (the same \emph{a} from \emph{arrivederci}).
  \item \textbf{domani} = \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{dē māne}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}from the morning.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{itemize}

That word \textbf{māne} (\textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}) is quietly shared across the Romance family, and you may have already met its Spanish child:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Italian \textbf{domani} (\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ \emph{dē māne}.
  \item Spanish \textbf{mañana} $\leftarrow$ \emph{(hōra) māneāna} — which means \textbf{both} \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} \emph{and} \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} because tomorrow \emph{is} \textquotedblleft{}the coming morning.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{a domani} literally says \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}until the morning {[}to come{]}.\textquotedblright{}} You part by pointing at daybreak.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a domani\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ah doh-MAH-nee}
  \item Italian \emph{domani} and Spanish \emph{mañana} — both from \emph{māne}, \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{domani} come from, and what does it literally mean? (\emph{Dē māne} — \textquotedblleft{}from the morning.\textquotedblright{}) Which Spanish word shares that \emph{māne} root? (\emph{Mañana} — morning \emph{and} tomorrow.) Next: \textquotedblleft{}see you soon\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{a presto}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a presto]{a presto — \textquotedblleft{}see you soon\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:IT-C04-a-presto}



\begin{quote}
Same frame, new \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}: \textbf{a presto}, \textquotedblleft{}to soon.\textquotedblright{} And \emph{presto} is a word English already borrowed whole — from stage magic and music.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a presto} = \emph{ah \textbf{PREH}-stoh}: clean \emph{st}, crisp open \emph{e}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a} = \textquotedblleft{}to / until.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{presto} = \textquotedblleft{}soon, quickly,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{praestō}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}at hand, ready, present\textquotedblright{}} (\emph{prae-} \textquotedblleft{}before\textquotedblright{} + \emph{stō/stāre} \textquotedblleft{}stand\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}standing before you,\textquotedblright{} ready to hand).
\end{itemize}

English took \textbf{presto} straight from Italian:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item in \textbf{music}, \emph{presto} means \textquotedblleft{}fast.\textquotedblright{}
  \item in stage magic, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}presto!\textquotedblright{}} means \textquotedblleft{}quick — and there it is!\textquotedblright{}
  \item it shares that \emph{stō} (\textquotedblleft{}stand\textquotedblright{}) root with \emph{stare} from your how-are-you chapter, and with English \textbf{station}, \textbf{stable}, \textbf{status}.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{a presto} is \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}until {[}it is{]} soon / at hand\textquotedblright{}} — see you before long.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a presto\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ah PREH-stoh}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}presto\textquotedblright{} as music (\textquotedblleft{}fast\textquotedblright{}) and magic (\textquotedblleft{}presto!\textquotedblright{}) — same word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{presto} mean, and where has English borrowed it? (\textquotedblleft{}Soon / quickly\textquotedblright{} — in music and magic.) What \textquotedblleft{}stand\textquotedblright{} root does it share with \emph{stare}? (Latin \emph{stō/stāre}.) Next: \textquotedblleft{}see you later\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{a più tardi}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a più tardi]{a più tardi — \textquotedblleft{}see you later\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:IT-C04-a-piu-tardi}



\begin{quote}
The last \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{} in the set: \textbf{a più tardi}, \textquotedblleft{}to later\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}to \emph{more late}.\textquotedblright{} Two small words, both alive in English.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{piu-glide} — \textbf{più} = \emph{pyoo}, one gliding syllable (the accent marks the stress).
  \item \textbf{a più tardi} = \emph{ah pyoo \textbf{TAR}-dee}, tapped \emph{r}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a} = \textquotedblleft{}to / until.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{più} = \textquotedblleft{}more,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{plūs} — the very word English took for \textbf{plus}, and the root of \textbf{plural}, \textbf{surplus}.
  \item \textbf{tardi} = \textquotedblleft{}late,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{tardus}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}slow, late\textquotedblright{}} $\to$ English \textbf{tardy}, \textbf{re-tard} (\textquotedblleft{}to slow down\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{tardy} slip.
\end{itemize}

Together, \emph{più tardi} = \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}more late\textquotedblright{}} = \textquotedblleft{}later.\textquotedblright{} So \emph{a più tardi} is \textquotedblleft{}until {[}it's{]} more-late\textquotedblright{} — see you later on. (Italian builds \textquotedblleft{}later\textquotedblright{} as \emph{more late}, just as English does with the comparative \emph{-er}.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a più tardi\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ah pyoo TAR-dee}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}più\textquotedblright{} \textasciitilde{} English \emph{plus}; \textquotedblleft{}tardi\textquotedblright{} \textasciitilde{} English \emph{tardy} — both borrowed
  \item the four goodbyes — arrivederci / a domani / a presto / a più tardi
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do \emph{più} and \emph{tardi} mean, and their English cousins? (\emph{Più} = \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{} \textasciitilde{} plus; \emph{tardi} = \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{} \textasciitilde{} tardy.) So \emph{a più tardi} literally says? (\textquotedblleft{}To more-late\textquotedblright{} $\to$ see you later.) Next: put the farewells together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — saying goodbye in Italian}

\label{lesson:IT-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. You can now open a conversation, ask how someone is, and \textbf{close} it. Run the goodbyes until the right one comes automatically.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the closings}
\textbf{Neutral / polite} (anyone):

\begin{quote}
— È stato un piacere. \textbf{Arrivederci!} — \textbf{Arrivederci!}
\end{quote}

\textbf{With a \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}} — pick the promise that fits:

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{A domani!} (see you tomorrow) — \textbf{A presto!} (see you soon) — \textbf{A più tardi!} (see you later — same day)
\end{quote}

\textbf{Casual} (a friend): the \emph{ciao} you learned in Chapter 1 doubles as \textquotedblleft{}bye\textquotedblright{} —

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Ciao, a presto!}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{arrivederci} — goodbye (\textquotedblleft{}until we re-see each other\textquotedblright{}; the \emph{au revoir} / \emph{auf Wiedersehen} family). Heavier, final variant: \textbf{addio} (\textquotedblleft{}to God,\textquotedblright{} twin of \emph{adiós}).
  \item \textbf{a domani} — see you tomorrow (\emph{domani} $\leftarrow$ \emph{dē māne}, \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}; kin of Spanish \emph{mañana}).
  \item \textbf{a presto} — see you soon (\emph{presto} $\leftarrow$ \emph{praestō}, \textquotedblleft{}at hand\textquotedblright{} — the English music/magic word).
  \item \textbf{a più tardi} — see you later (\emph{più} \textasciitilde{} plus, \emph{tardi} \textasciitilde{} tardy).
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item greet, ask, and close — \textquotedblleft{}Ciao! Come stai? … A domani!\textquotedblright{}
  \item choose the right goodbye — leaving till tomorrow / in an hour / for good
  \item arrivederci / au revoir / auf Wiedersehen — the \textquotedblleft{}re-seeing\textquotedblright{} trio
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Open and close a whole tiny exchange without stopping.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which goodbye means \textquotedblleft{}until we see each other again\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Arrivederci}.) Which says \textquotedblleft{}to the morning\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{A domani}.) Which Italian goodbye matches Spanish \emph{adiós} — \textquotedblleft{}to God\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Addio}.) You can now run an Italian conversation start to finish.
\end{tcolorbox}
